weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies standard bi-encoder + listwise reranking to a new task without methodological innovations. The modified training objective (first-token prediction) is a pragmatic workaround lacking principled justification

strengths: Clear problem motivation: Identifies a real gap where agent-based approaches are expensive (~$0.66/example) and brittle, while traditional code ranking models aren't optimized for verbose issue descriptions

Strong empirical results: Outperforms all baselines including LocAgent with Claude-3.5 (83.21% vs 77.74% file Acc@1) while achieving 6× better cost-to-accuracy ratio

Comprehensive experimental analysis: Thorough ablations on data quality and size, evaluation across multiple granularities (file, module, function) and benchmarks, with clear cost-effectiveness analysis
Practical approach: Retrieve-and-rerank framework avoids brittleness of agentic systems from sampling and tool orchestration failures, enabling reliable deployment
Dataset utility demonstrated: Tables 3-4 show SWELOC benefits diverse retriever and reranker models, establishing it as a valuable community resource
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Core contributions apply standard techniques (InfoNCE contrastive loss, established listwise reranking) to a new domain; data filtering and hard negative mining adapted from Suresh et al. (2024)
Ad-hoc listwise training adaptation: Simplifying to predict only the top token (Section 4.2) lacks principled justification and ablation studies comparing to full ranking supervision
Insufficient justification of hyperparameters: Choices like K=20, different hard negatives/epochs for SMALL vs LARGE variants, and query truncation strategy are not well explained or ablated
Limited evaluation scope: Only two relatively small benchmarks (274 and 560 examples); all evaluation on Python only with no analysis of generalization to other languages or non-GitHub sources
Missing error analysis and failure investigation: Figure 4 shows poor performance on 'Performance Issues' (~45% function Acc@15) but this isn't discussed; no comprehensive failure mode analysis
Data leakage risks not fully addressed: Pre-trained models (CodeRankEmbed, GTE-Qwen2) may have seen similar GitHub code; no analysis of overlap with pre-training corpora
Insufficient reproducibility details: No random seeds or variance reporting; GH200 GPUs are not widely accessible; some hyperparameter choices appear empirically driven without principled selection
Limited analysis of learned representations: No embedding visualization, attention analysis for SWERANKLLM, or investigation of what patterns the models learn

Sound technical approach with principled contrastive learning (InfoNCE), clever adaptation of listwise reranking for partial supervision, and detailed reproducible training procedures
Compelling motivation addressing real limitations of agent-based approaches (high cost, latency, brittleness) with pragmatic alternative

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical value; articulates genuine limitations of agent-based approaches (cost, latency, brittleness)

Strong practical results: 6× better performance-cost tradeoffs vs LocAgent, 7× faster inference, achieves SOTA on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench
Useful dataset contribution (SWELOC): 67k examples with careful quality control (consistency filtering, hard-negative mining); publicly released and demonstrates cross-lingual generalization
Thorough downstream analysis showing impact on code repair performance and detailed performance stratification by issue characteristics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: retriever uses standard bi-encoder with InfoNCE loss; reranker employs simplified training that only predicts top-1 positive ID rather than full ranking, justified as necessity but is actually a design choice that could use semantic similarity or weak labels

Small benchmark scale (274 SWE-Bench-Lite, 560 LocBench examples) with no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars; high variance possible

Methodological concern: using CODERANKEMBED to filter the dataset then fine-tuning SWERANKEMBED on filtered data creates potential circularity/bias; filter and target models should be independent

Dense presentation with critical results relegated to appendix (Tables 3-4, 7-11; Figures 5-8); main text lacks depth in key methodological sections

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a clear practical bottleneck: agent-based issue localization is expensive (~$0.66/example) and slow (7-10 interaction rounds), while existing code ranking models aren't optimized for verbose, failure-descriptive issue descriptions

Substantial dataset contribution (SWELOC): 67,341 carefully curated GitHub issue-code pairs with principled three-stage construction (PR filtering, localization processing, quality filtering), consistency filtering (K=20), and hard-negative mining (M=15)

Exceptional empirical results: achieves SOTA on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench across all granularities (file/module/function), outperforms LocAgent (Claude-3.5), and demonstrates 6× better cost-efficiency and 7× faster latency than agent-based methods

Thorough and comprehensive experimental evaluation: extensive ablations on data quality/size, analysis by issue complexity and semantic overlap, downstream impact on code repair, multilingual generalization (works across 9 languages despite Python-only training), and detailed efficiency analysis (latency, tokens, inference cost)

Sound technical approach with clever pragmatic adaptations: modified listwise reranker training (Eq. 2) elegantly handles setting where only positive labels are known, avoiding need for full ranking supervision; appropriate use of InfoNCE contrastive loss
Strong reproducibility and clarity: training details provided in appendices, clear methodology description, promised code/model release, and generally well-written presentation with good motivation
Demonstrated generalizability: SWELOC improves performance across diverse pre-trained retrievers and rerankers (Table 3-4), validating dataset value for the community
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: bi-encoder retriever uses standard InfoNCE loss, listwise reranking adapted from prior work (Reddy et al., 2024), consistency filtering and hard-negative mining follow Suresh et al. (2024). Core contribution is more problem/dataset-focused than methodologically novel

Dataset construction concerns: Python-only training data (multilingual generalization only on evaluation), exact size after filtering unclear (67,341 initial pairs reduced by consistency filtering but final count not explicitly stated), assumes all modified functions in a PR are relevant to the issue (potential label noise)

Limited evaluation scope: restricted to two benchmarks both derived from SWE-Bench (limited diversity), agent baselines use closed-source models (Claude-3.5, GPT-4o) while SWERANK uses open-source (unequal comparison), missing open-source agent baselines and traditional IR methods (e.g., TF-IDF)

Training-inference discrepancy: reranker trained to predict only top-ranked identifier (Eq. 2) but generates full ranking at inference; explanation in Section 4.2 regarding end-of-sequence token omission is brief and could be clearer

Insufficient analysis of learned patterns and failure modes: limited insight into why issue-code mappings are learned; no attention analysis or representation visualization; only two qualitative examples; no systematic analysis of failure cases or difficult issue categories

Scalability concerns underexplored: dense embedding computation and storage costs for very large codebases not discussed; impact of context window constraints (16K tokens) on large code files unclear; no discussion of deployment to monorepos with millions of functions

Data licensing and ethical considerations not addressed: no discussion of GitHub data privacy, licensing compliance, or consent for reuse in commercial systems; unclear if SWELOC release includes proper attributions

Cost comparison not entirely fair: Table 5 costs drawn from different sources rather than consistent direct measurements; comparison with agent approaches that use closed-source expensive models makes SWERANK look better but doesn't control for model choice
